title: Safer definitions of free choice: those of Alvarez and of Bellarmine
source_text: XLIII. Itaque vulgata illa descriptione Liberi Arbitrii per quam definitur facultas qua positis omnibus ad agendum praerequisitis, potest aliquis agere & non agere, hoc aut illud agere, tutior est ea quam substituit Alvarez, Liberum arbitrium est facultas voluntatis & rationis ad utrum libet agendum vel non agendum & agendum unum vel alterum. Aut etiam illa Bellarmini, Liberum arbitrium est libera potestas ex his quae ad finem aliquem conducunt unum prae alio eligendi, aut unum & idem respuendi vel acceptandi pro arbitrio nostro, ad magnam Dei gloriam attributa vel concessa.
pass_a_gloss: Therefore than that common description of Free Choice by which it is defined a faculty by which, all things prerequisite to acting being posited, one can act and not act, do this or that, safer is that which Alvarez substituted, Free choice is a faculty of the will and of reason to acting or not acting whichever one pleases and to doing one or the other. Or also that of Bellarmine, Free choice is a free power of choosing, out of those things which conduce to some end, one before another, or of rejecting or accepting one and the same thing at our choice, attributed or granted for the great glory of God.
pass_b_english: So, rather than the familiar description of free choice as 'a faculty by which, given everything required beforehand for acting, a person can act and not act, do this or that', it is safer to use the one Alvarez put in its place: 'Free choice is a faculty of will and reason for acting or not acting, as one pleases, and for doing one thing or the other.'

Or else Bellarmine's: 'Free choice is a free power, given or granted for the great glory of God, to choose one thing over another among the things that lead to some end, or to reject or accept one and the same thing as we decide.'

choices.why: Kept as in the preceding locus on free choice in general, so the Roman and Reformed accounts are compared in one vocabulary.
